description: I’m Francesco, a Master’s student with a business and innovation background and a big passion for space. I’m taking on the lunar south pole landing site challenge. I have the idea, the plan and the data ready, but I’d really love a teammate to build it with, especially someone comfortable with Python, web development or design. No need to be an expert, just curious and motivated. Let’s make it happen together!
summary: Lunar Site Scout is a free web app that tells a mission where and when to land near the Moon's south pole, and why. At the pole the Sun and Earth skim the horizon, so a nearby ridge decides whether a lander gets power and a link to Earth. Our app shows the real Sun and Earth over the real NASA terrain horizon at 11 sites, for any date, so planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds. For a specific mission it checks every site every 6 hours in the worst case and gives a clear Go / No-go verdict on sunlight, power, battery, Earth contact and cost, with a PDF report and an Excel file showing every source.
details:
Landing near the Moon's south pole is one of the hardest choices in space exploration. The Sun and Earth stay low on the horizon, so a single ridge can leave a lander without power or without contact with Earth, as the IM-2 lander found out in 2025.

Lunar Site Scout makes that choice simple. It is a free web app where anyone can fly over the south pole in 3D, see the real Sun and Earth in the sky on any date, and stand on a landing site next to a real-size lander. Mission teams can bring their own mission, as a PDF or by answering 8 questions, and in seconds the app compares 11 sites over time and explains the best place and day to land: sunlight, battery, contact with Earth and cost, always in the worst case. For Griffin-1, the best site avoids 31 kg of extra battery and about $41 million compared with the next one.

We wanted two faces of the same Moon: playful and educational for students and the public, precise and practical for engineers, agencies and companies. Both use the same NASA terrain and JPL data, checked against JPL Horizons, and every number in the PDF and Excel reports shows its source.

We built it with Python for the data and JavaScript with three.js for the 3D app. It runs in any browser, phone included, and documents never leave the user's device. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code and texts; the team designed, reviewed and tested every result.
